stimuli.title: Twelve persons in two facing rows of six
stimuli.content:
Twelve persons Arya, Bhola, Chanda, Dhiren, Gulab, Hasan, Kapil, Lalit, Mohan, Nayan, Ravi and Tulsi sit in two parallel rows of six seats each. The persons in Row 1 face south and those in Row 2 face north, so each person faces exactly one person of the other row. (Facing south, the right is towards the west; facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Mohan sits in Row 1, third from the east end of that row.
- Hasan faces Mohan, and Bhola sits immediately to the right of Hasan.
- Tulsi sits immediately to the right of Mohan, and Dhiren faces Tulsi.
- Ravi sits second to the left of Mohan, and Gulab sits between Mohan and Ravi.
- Lalit faces Ravi, and Chanda sits at one end of Row 2.
- Nayan faces Arya, who sits in the row that faces south.
stimuli.solution:
Number the columns 1 to 6 from the west in both rows.
Step 1: Mohan = Row 1, column 4. Hasan faces him: Row 2, column 4; Bhola, to Hasan's right (east): Row 2, column 5.
Step 2: Tulsi, to Mohan's right (west): Row 1, column 3; Dhiren faces her: Row 2, column 3.
Step 3: Ravi, second to Mohan's left (east): Row 1, column 6; Gulab between them: column 5. Lalit faces Ravi: Row 2, column 6, so Chanda is at the other end: Row 2, column 1.
Step 4: Free seats: Row 1 columns 1 and 2, Row 2 column 2. Nayan faces Arya, so they take the facing pair Row 2 column 2 and Row 1 column 2; Arya is in the south-facing Row 1, so Nayan is in Row 2, and Kapil gets Row 1, column 1.

| Column | Row 1 (facing south) | Row 2 (facing north) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kapil | Chanda |
| 2 | Arya | Nayan |
| 3 | Tulsi | Dhiren |
| 4 | Mohan | Hasan |
| 5 | Gulab | Bhola |
| 6 | Ravi | Lalit |

stimuli.content:

- Fuzail sits immediately to the left of Dolu.
- Esha and Gita sit in adjacent seats, Esha to the left of Gita, and exactly one seat lies between Bhim and Esha.

Step 2: One seat lies between Bhim (1) and Esha: Esha = 3, and Gita, immediately to her right, = 4.
Step 3: The vacant seats are 2, 5 and 8.

stimuli.title: Eight persons in a row, ranked by height
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Hiran, Ishu, Kuku, Lado, Mitu, Nanki, Pammi and Rinku sit in a straight row, all facing north. No two of them are of the same height. (Facing north, the right is towards the east.)

- Lado and Pammi sit at the two ends of the row, Lado at the left end.
- The tallest person sits immediately to the right of Lado, and the shortest person sits immediately to the right of the tallest person.
- Nanki is the second tallest and sits second to the right of the tallest person.
- Hiran sits second to the right of Nanki and is shorter than only Kuku and Nanki.
- Kuku is taller than Nanki.
- Ishu sits immediately to the left of Hiran, and Rinku immediately to the right of Hiran.
- Ishu is shorter than everyone except the shortest person; Rinku is taller than Lado, and Lado is taller than Pammi.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 1 to 8 from the left.
Step 1: Lado = 1, Pammi = 8. The tallest person is on seat 2 and the shortest on seat 3. Nanki (2nd tallest) = 4, Hiran (3rd tallest) = 6, Ishu = 5, Rinku = 7.
Step 2: Kuku and Mitu take seats 2 and 3. Kuku is taller than Nanki, the second tallest, so Kuku is the tallest (seat 2) and Mitu the shortest (seat 3).
Step 3: Ranks 4 to 7 remain for Ishu, Rinku, Lado and Pammi. Ishu is 7th; Rinku > Lado > Pammi in height: Rinku 4th, Lado 5th, Pammi 6th.

| Seat | Person | Height rank |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lado | 5 |
| 2 | Kuku | 1 |
| 3 | Mitu | 8 |
| 4 | Nanki | 2 |
| 5 | Ishu | 7 |
| 6 | Hiran | 3 |
| 7 | Rinku | 4 |
| 8 | Pammi | 6 |

stimuli.title: Ten chairs, eight persons
stimuli.content:
Ten chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Eight persons Ajay, Bimal, Disha, Fateh, Jassi, Lucky, Rupal and Ujjal sit on eight of them, all facing the centre; two chairs are vacant. Positions such as 'second to the right' count chairs, including vacant ones. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise.)

- Jassi sits opposite Ajay, and Bimal sits immediately to the left of Jassi.
- Rupal sits immediately to the right of Ajay. Fateh sits second to the right of Rupal, and the chair between Rupal and Fateh is vacant.
- Lucky sits immediately to the left of Ajay, and Disha sits immediately to the left of Lucky.
- Ujjal sits immediately to the right of Jassi.
- The two vacant chairs are exactly opposite each other.
stimuli.solution:
Number the chairs 0 to 9 anticlockwise from Ajay.
Step 1: Jassi = 5 (opposite), Bimal = 4 (Jassi's left, clockwise), Ujjal = 6.
Step 2: Rupal = 1, chair 2 is vacant, Fateh = 3.
Step 3: Lucky = 9, Disha = 8. The only chair left is 7, which is vacant — and it is exactly opposite chair 2, as required.

|---|---|

| 1 | Rupal |
| 2 | vacant |
| 3 | Fateh |
| 4 | Bimal |
| 5 | Jassi |

stimuli.title: Seven persons facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Rohit, Saloni, Tanuj, Urvi, Vedika, Xena and Yuvi sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (Facing the centre, the right is anticlockwise; facing outside, it is clockwise.)

- Rohit faces the centre, and Urvi sits immediately to his right.
- Urvi faces outside, and Yuvi sits immediately to Urvi's left.
- Saloni sits immediately to the right of Yuvi, and the two of them face opposite directions.
- Vedika sits immediately to the left of Rohit and faces the same direction as Rohit.
- Tanuj sits immediately to the left of Vedika.
- Xena faces the centre, Xena and Tanuj face opposite directions, and Yuvi faces the same direction as Xena.
stimuli.solution:
Number the seats 0 to 6 anticlockwise from Rohit.
Step 1: Rohit faces the centre: Urvi = 1. Urvi faces outside, so her left is anticlockwise: Yuvi = 2.
Step 2: Vedika, on Rohit's left (clockwise), = 6 and faces the centre. Tanuj, on Vedika's left, = 5.
Step 3: Xena faces the centre; Yuvi faces the same way (centre), Tanuj the other way (outside). Saloni faces opposite to Yuvi (outside) and sits on Yuvi's right (anticlockwise): 3. Xena takes seat 4.

| Seat | Person | Facing |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Rohit | facing the centre |
| 1 | Urvi | facing outside |
| 2 | Yuvi | facing the centre |
| 3 | Saloni | facing outside |
| 4 | Xena | facing the centre |
| 5 | Tanuj | facing outside |
| 6 | Vedika | facing the centre |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six hobbies
stimuli.content:
Six persons Bablu, Chameli, Dinu, Ganesh, Heena and Jagan live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 6 the topmost). Each has a different hobby among Dancing, Painting, Reading, Singing, Swimming and Writing.

- Chameli lives on floor 4, Bablu immediately above her and Jagan immediately below her.
- Dinu lives on the topmost floor, and Heena lives below Ganesh.
- The person who likes Painting lives on an even-numbered floor between Jagan and Bablu.
- The person on the topmost floor likes Singing, and the person on floor 1 likes Reading.
- The person who likes Dancing lives immediately below the person who likes Painting.
- Bablu does not like Swimming.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Chameli = 4, Bablu = 5, Jagan = 3, Dinu = 6. Floors 1 and 2 remain; Heena is below Ganesh: Heena = 1, Ganesh = 2.
Step 2: Painting is on an even floor between 3 and 5: floor 4 (Chameli). Dancing is immediately below: floor 3 (Jagan). Singing: floor 6 (Dinu). Reading: floor 1 (Heena).
Step 3: Swimming and Writing remain for Ganesh and Bablu; Bablu does not swim: Bablu Writing, Ganesh Swimming.

| Floor | Person | Hobby |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Dinu | Singing |
| 5 | Bablu | Writing |
| 4 | Chameli | Painting |
| 3 | Jagan | Dancing |
| 2 | Ganesh | Swimming |
| 1 | Heena | Reading |

stimuli.title: Two persons on each of four floors, with colours
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Arif, Chinki, Gudiya, Hanif, Lalu, Mamta, Pintu and Sweety live in a four-storey building, two persons on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost, floor 4 the topmost). Each likes a different colour among Amber, Coral, Indigo, Lilac, Mint, Navy, Rose and Tan.

- Gudiya lives on floor 3 and likes Rose.
- Arif lives on the floor immediately above Gudiya's and likes Mint.
- Hanif lives on an even-numbered floor below Gudiya.
- Chinki and Mamta live on the same floor.
- Sweety lives above Lalu, and Pintu lives on the floor immediately below Lalu's.
- The person who likes Navy lives on the topmost floor. Hanif likes Amber and Pintu likes Lilac.
- The person who likes Tan lives on floor 3, and Chinki does not like Indigo.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: Gudiya = 3 (Rose), Arif = 4 (Mint), Hanif = 2 (Amber).
Step 2: Chinki and Mamta share a floor; floors 2, 3 and 4 each have only one free place, so they live on floor 1.
Step 3: Lalu, Pintu and Sweety fill one place each on floors 2, 3 and 4. Pintu is immediately below Lalu and Sweety is above Lalu: Pintu = 2, Lalu = 3, Sweety = 4.
Step 4: Navy is on floor 4; Arif likes Mint, so Sweety likes Navy. Pintu likes Lilac. Tan is on floor 3, where Gudiya likes Rose, so Lalu likes Tan. Coral and Indigo remain for Chinki and Mamta; Chinki does not like Indigo: Chinki Coral, Mamta Indigo.

| Floor | Persons (colour) |
|---|---|
| 4 | Arif (Mint), Sweety (Navy) |
| 3 | Gudiya (Rose), Lalu (Tan) |
| 2 | Hanif (Amber), Pintu (Lilac) |
| 1 | Chinki (Coral), Mamta (Indigo) |

stimuli.title: A basement, a ground floor and six floors
stimuli.content:
A building has a basement, a ground floor and six floors above the ground floor (floors 1 to 6, floor 6 being the topmost). Eight persons Abhi, Barun, Chaya, Dilip, Emily, Feroz, Gagan and Harsha live in it, one on each of these eight levels. Each has a different profession among Actor, Baker, Cashier, Doctor, Editor, Farmer, Guard and Nurse. 'Level' means any of the eight (basement, ground floor or floor 1-6).

- Exactly three persons live above Emily, and Emily is the Actor.
- The Doctor lives two levels below Emily.
- Chaya lives on the ground floor, immediately above the Guard.
- Barun lives on the topmost floor, and Dilip lives two levels below Barun.
- Gagan lives between Dilip and Barun.
- Feroz lives below Harsha, and Abhi lives immediately above Harsha.
- The Nurse lives immediately above the Doctor.
- The Cashier lives immediately below the Editor, and the Editor lives below the Farmer.
stimuli.solution:
List the levels from the bottom: basement, ground, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Step 1: Three persons live above Emily, so Emily is on floor 3 (the Actor). The Doctor is two levels lower: floor 1.
Step 2: Chaya = ground floor; the Guard is in the basement. Barun = floor 6, Dilip = floor 4, Gagan = floor 5.
Step 3: Feroz, Harsha and Abhi take the basement, floor 1 and floor 2. Abhi is immediately above Harsha and Feroz below Harsha: Feroz = basement (Guard), Harsha = floor 1 (Doctor), Abhi = floor 2.
Step 4: The Nurse is immediately above the Doctor: Abhi. Baker, Cashier, Editor and Farmer remain for Chaya (ground), Dilip (4), Gagan (5) and Barun (6). Cashier is immediately below Editor, and Editor is below Farmer: Cashier 4 (Dilip), Editor 5 (Gagan), Farmer 6 (Barun). Chaya is the Baker.

|---|---|---|
| floor 6 | Barun | Farmer |
| floor 5 | Gagan | Editor |
| floor 4 | Dilip | Cashier |
| floor 3 | Emily | Actor |
| floor 2 | Abhi | Nurse |
| floor 1 | Harsha | Doctor |
| the ground floor | Chaya | Baker |
| the basement | Feroz | Guard |

stimuli.title: Eight coloured boxes in a stack
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes A, C, E, H, K, N, R and W are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 8 the top). Each box is of a different colour among Aqua, Black, Cyan, Gold, Ivory, Lime, Plum and Rust.

- Box A is kept fourth from the bottom and is Black; Box N is kept immediately above Box A.
- Box K is kept at the top, and Box H is kept immediately below Box K.
- Box C is kept between Box N and Box H, and Box R is kept at the bottom.
- Box W is kept above Box E.
- The Ivory box is kept immediately above the Black box, and the top box is Cyan.
- The Gold box is kept two places below the Black box, and the Plum box is kept between the Gold and Black boxes.
- The Rust box is kept immediately below the Cyan box, and the bottom box is not Aqua.
stimuli.solution:
Step 1: A = 4 (Black), N = 5, K = 8, H = 7, C = 6, R = 1.
Step 2: Positions 2 and 3 remain for E and W; W is above E: E = 2, W = 3.
Step 3: Ivory = 5 (N), Cyan = 8 (K), Gold = 2 (E), Plum = 3 (W), Rust = 7 (H).
Step 4: Aqua and Lime remain for R (1) and C (6); the bottom box is not Aqua: R Lime, C Aqua.

stimuli.title: Eight boxes on two shelves
stimuli.content:
Eight boxes B, D, F, H, J, L, N and P are placed on two shelves, upper and lower, four boxes on each shelf in a line. Each box on the upper shelf is directly above one box on the lower shelf. Left and right are as seen from the front.

- Box L is immediately to the right of Box F, and Box B is directly above Box L.
- Box H is at the left end of the lower shelf, and Box P is on the lower shelf.

stimuli.title: Seven boxes of three sizes
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes C, G, M, Q, T, V and Y are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom). Three boxes are Large, two Medium and two Small.

- No box is kept directly on top of a box smaller than itself.
- Box Y is Medium, and Box C is kept immediately below Box Y.
- Box M is kept at the top, and Box T is Small.
- Box G is kept immediately below Box T.
- Box V is kept below Box Q.

Step 2: M = 7 (Small). T is Small: T = 6, and G, immediately below T, = 5 (Medium).
Step 3: Y is Medium: the only Medium place left is 4, so Y = 4 and C = 3 (Large).
Step 4: V and Q take 1 and 2 with V below: V = 1, Q = 2.

stimuli.title: Five filled and hollow shapes for comparisons
stimuli.content:
In the questions of this set, five shapes are used between two letters with these meanings:
'A ◆ B' means 'A is greater than B'; 'A ◇ B' means 'A is either greater than or equal to B'; 'A ▼ B' means 'A is smaller than B'; 'A ▽ B' means 'A is either smaller than or equal to B'; 'A ○ B' means 'A is equal to B'.
Assuming the statements to be true, find which of the conclusions I and II is/are definitely true.
stimuli.solution: Decode: ◆ means >, ◇ means ≥, ▼ means <, ▽ means ≤ and ○ means =. Rewrite the statements with ordinary signs, join them into a chain and test each conclusion.

stimuli.title: Five children and their chocolates
stimuli.content:
Five children Golu, Hiya, Jojo, Kiku and Lalli have different numbers of chocolates.

- Hiya has more chocolates than Golu but fewer than Kiku.
- Jojo has fewer chocolates than Golu.
- Lalli has more chocolates than Kiku.
stimuli.solution: Golu < Hiya < Kiku < Lalli, and Jojo < Golu. Order (most first): Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo.

stimuli.title: Six school posts and six subjects
stimuli.content:
Six teachers Kamini, Lokesh, Madhav, Naina, Oorja and Pratik of a school hold six different posts. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Principal, Vice-Principal, Coordinator, Senior Teacher, Teacher and Assistant Teacher. Each teaches a different subject among Maths, Science, English, History, Art and Music.

- The Maths teacher is senior to exactly four of the others.
- The History teacher is the Principal.
- Kamini is junior to the Maths teacher but senior to Pratik.
- Lokesh is the most junior, and he teaches neither Music nor Art.
- Pratik teaches Science, and Naina teaches Music and is junior to Pratik.
- Madhav is senior to Oorja.
- The Art teacher is senior to the Science teacher.
stimuli.solution:
The Maths teacher has four people below: Vice-Principal. The Principal teaches History. Lokesh is the Assistant Teacher (rank 6). Pratik teaches Science and Naina Music, Naina junior to Pratik; Kamini is junior to the Vice-Principal but senior to Pratik. So Kamini > Pratik > Naina > Lokesh fills ranks 3 to 6: Kamini Coordinator, Pratik Senior Teacher, Naina Teacher. Madhav and Oorja take ranks 1 and 2, Madhav senior: Madhav Principal (History), Oorja Vice-Principal (Maths). Lokesh teaches neither Music nor Art, so English; Kamini teaches Art (and is senior to the Science teacher, as required).

Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Assistant Teacher–English.

stimuli.solution: Decode pair by pair from the left; the parents of a child are a married couple.

stimuli.title: A family described in three codes
stimuli.content:
In a certain code, 'A ⊕ B' means 'A is a parent of B', 'A ⊗ B' means 'A is married to B' and 'A ⊖ B' means 'A and B are siblings'. Kartik, Mehul, Pranav and Qasim are male; Leela, Naina, Ojasvi and Riya are female. The following are true:

- Kartik ⊗ Leela
- Leela ⊕ Mehul
- Mehul ⊖ Naina
- Ojasvi ⊗ Mehul
- Ojasvi ⊕ Pranav
- Qasim ⊗ Naina
- Qasim ⊕ Riya
stimuli.solution:
Leela, Kartik's wife, is a parent of Mehul, and Naina is Mehul's sibling, so both are children of Kartik and Leela. Ojasvi is Mehul's wife and Pranav's mother; Qasim is Naina's husband and Riya's parent.
Tree: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya.

stimuli.title: A taxi's route with five stops
stimuli.content: A taxi leaves its depot D and drives in straight lines: 6 km east to stop A, then 8 km north to stop B, then 12 km west to stop C, then 5 km south to stop E, and finally 10 km east to stop F, where it ends its trip.
stimuli.solution: With D at (0, 0), east and north positive: A (6, 0), B (6, 8), C (−6, 8), E (−6, 3), F (4, 3).

stimuli.title: Six points with a midpoint

Six points J, K, L, M, N and O lie on flat ground.

- L is 10 m north of J.
- M is the midpoint of the straight line joining K and L.

stimuli.title: A three-part code that depends on word length
stimuli.content:
In a certain code, a word is written as: its last letter, then the number of letters in the word, then the letter that comes two places after its first letter in the English alphabet. If the word has an even number of letters, the whole code is then written in reverse order.
For example, TRAIN is written as N5V and HOME is written as J4E.
stimuli.solution: Odd length: last letter + length + (first letter + 2). Even length: the same three parts, reversed.

stimuli.content:

stimuli.title: A row of unknown length
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a row, all facing north.

- Arun is 8th from the left end.
- Bela sits to the right of Arun, and exactly five persons sit between Arun and Bela.
- Chetan sits third to the left of Bela.
- Exactly four persons sit between Chetan and Dinesh, and Dinesh sits to the right of Bela.
- Dinesh is 4th from the right end of the row.
stimuli.solution: From the left: Arun 8th, Bela 8 + 6 = 14th, Chetan 14 − 3 = 11th. Dinesh is five places from Chetan (6th or 16th) and to the right of Bela, so 16th; being 4th from the right, the row has 16 + 4 − 1 = 19 persons.

stimuli.title: Machine: second letters to the right
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word whose SECOND letter comes earliest in the alphabet, and places it at the right end, immediately to the left of the words already arranged there (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other words keep their order. A step that would not change the line is not counted, and the machine stops when the arrangement is complete.

Input: drum flute horn piano tabla veena guitar
stimuli.solution:
Second letters: drum r, flute l, horn o, piano i, tabla a, veena e, guitar u. Order of selection: tabla, veena, piano, flute, horn, drum, guitar.

Step I: drum flute horn piano veena guitar tabla
Step II: drum flute horn piano guitar veena tabla
Step III: drum flute horn guitar piano veena tabla
Step IV: drum horn guitar flute piano veena tabla
Step V: drum guitar horn flute piano veena tabla
Step VI: guitar drum horn flute piano veena tabla

stimuli.title: Machine: halve or add three, then rotate
stimuli.content:
A number machine changes a line of numbers step by step. In each step it first replaces every number: an odd number by that number plus 3, and an even number by half of it. It then moves the number at the left end of the line to the right end; the other numbers keep their order. The machine runs for four steps.

Input: 36 15 48 27 64 9

stimuli.title: Machine: words and numbers in turn
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step, moving one element per step. In Steps I, III, V, … it takes, among the words not yet arranged, the word that comes last in alphabetical order and places it at the left end, immediately to the right of the words already placed there. In Steps II, IV, VI, … it takes the smallest number not yet arranged, reverses its digits, and places the result at the right end, immediately to the left of the numbers already placed there. All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

Input: 81 lime jade 52 mint 37 rose 46
stimuli.solution:
Words in order: rose, mint, lime, jade. Numbers in order: 37 → 73, 46 → 64, 52 → 25, 81 → 18.

Step I: rose 81 lime jade 52 mint 37 46
Step II: rose 81 lime jade 52 mint 46 73
Step III: rose mint 81 lime jade 52 46 73
Step IV: rose mint 81 lime jade 52 64 73
Step V: rose mint lime 81 jade 52 64 73
Step VI: rose mint lime 81 jade 25 64 73
Step VII: rose mint lime jade 81 25 64 73
Step VIII: rose mint lime jade 18 25 64 73

steps: Chitti O ⇒ Navami C ⇒ Jalaj C ⇒ Hoshang O

questions.question_text:
Statements: N ≥ X; X > Q; Q ≤ V; V = H; H < E; A ≤ N

Conclusions:
I. N > Q
II. E > Q
III. E > V

Which of the conclusions is/are definitely true?

options.text: All I, II and III are true
Only I and II are true
Only II and III are true
Only I and III are true

solution.concept: Three conclusions tested against one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: A ≤ N ≥ X > Q ≤ V = H < E. N ≥ X > Q gives N > Q (I); E > H = V ≥ Q gives E > Q (II); E > H = V gives E > V (III). All three are true.
steps: Chain: A ≤ N ≥ X > Q ≤ V = H < E
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options drops one conclusion that does follow; none of I, II, III crosses the turn at Q.
solution.final_answer: Option A: All I, II and III are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which of the following expressions is 'R > D' definitely true and 'R > K' definitely false?

solution.concept: Two requirements at once: one relation forced, another impossible
solution.explanation: In K ≥ M = R > S ≥ D, R > S ≥ D gives R > D, and K ≥ M = R gives R ≤ K, so R > K can never hold.
steps: Need R > D forced and R ≤ K forced
K ≥ M = R ⇒ R ≤ K; R > S ≥ D ⇒ R > D
solution.why_others_wrong: R > M ≥ D = S ≥ K makes R > K true; in K > M ≤ R > S ≥ D and D < S = R ≥ M ≤ K, R and K are separated by a turn at M, so R > K is possible rather than definitely false.
solution.final_answer: Option B: K ≥ M = R > S ≥ D

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five friends Arpita, Bhola, Chinmay, Dimple and Elvis have their birthdays in five different months from August to December, one in each month.
- Chinmay's birthday is in October.
- Bhola's birthday is in a 30-day month before Chinmay's.
- Dimple's birthday is three months after Arpita's.

Whose birthday is in November?

solution.explanation: Chinmay: October. Bhola: the 30-day month before October in the range is September. Dimple is three months after Arpita: of August, November and December, only August → November works. Elvis takes December. November: Dimple.
solution.why_others_wrong: Elvis is in December, Arpita in August and Bhola in September.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Payal borrowed a library book on 27 January 2027 and returned it 9 days later. On the day Payal returned it, Qasim borrowed the same book and kept it for 12 days.

On which date did Qasim return the book?

solution.concept: Adding days across a month end
solution.explanation: January has 31 days: 27 January + 4 days = 31 January, and 5 more days give 5 February (Payal's return). Qasim: 5 February + 12 days = 17 February.
solution.why_others_wrong: 16 February and 18 February are one day off (counting 11 or 13 days for Qasim); 14 February treats January as a 28-day month.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
1 January 2026 is a Thursday, and 2026 is not a leap year. Five friends each guess the next year after 2026 whose calendar is exactly the same as that of 2026 (every date falling on the same day of the week): Kavin says 2032, Leela says 2037, Mehr says 2043 and Nagesh says 2036.

Whose guess is correct?

solution.concept: Odd days: +1 for an ordinary year, +2 after a leap year
solution.explanation: A calendar repeats when 1 January falls on the same weekday and the year is of the same type (ordinary). Moving from one 1 January to the next adds 1 weekday after an ordinary year and 2 after a leap year: 2027 Fri, 2028 Sat (leap), 2029 Mon, 2030 Tue, 2031 Wed, 2032 Thu — but 2032 is a leap year, so its calendar differs after February. 2033 Sat, 2034 Sun, 2035 Mon, 2036 Tue (leap), 2037 Thu, ordinary: 2037 repeats 2026.
steps: 1 Jan weekday: 2027 Fri, 2028 Sat, 2029 Mon, 2030 Tue, 2031 Wed, 2032 Thu (leap ✗)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2032 starts on a Thursday but is a leap year; 2043 also repeats 2026 but is not the next one; 2036 starts on a Tuesday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who has the most chocolates?

solution.explanation: Lalli has more than Kiku, who has more than everyone else.
steps: Most to fewest: Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo
solution.why_others_wrong: Kiku is second, Hiya third and Golu fourth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who is exactly in the middle of the order?

solution.explanation: Third of five: Hiya.
steps: Most to fewest: Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo
solution.why_others_wrong: Golu is fourth, Kiku second and Jojo fifth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many children have fewer chocolates than Kiku?

solution.explanation: Hiya, Golu and Jojo: three.
steps: Most to fewest: Lalli, Kiku, Hiya, Golu, Jojo
solution.why_others_wrong: Two misses Jojo or Golu; Four includes Lalli, who has more; One counts only Hiya.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four doctors Sunil, Tanu, Varsha and Yusra hold four posts in a hospital. In decreasing order of seniority the posts are: Medical Superintendent, Chief Medical Officer, Senior Resident and Junior Resident.
- Varsha is senior to Tanu but junior to Yusra.
- Sunil is not the Medical Superintendent.
- Tanu is not the most junior.

Who is the Senior Resident?

solution.explanation: Yusra > Varsha > Tanu. Tanu is not the most junior, so Sunil is the Junior Resident and Tanu the Senior Resident; Varsha is the CMO and Yusra the Medical Superintendent (Sunil is not).
steps: Tanu not last ⇒ Sunil Junior Resident
solution.why_others_wrong: Varsha is the CMO, Sunil the Junior Resident and Yusra the Medical Superintendent.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Asha, Babu, Chand, Dolly, Elan and Fatima each go to a swimming pool on one of six days from Sunday to Friday of the same week, one person per day.
- Chand goes on Tuesday, and Babu on the day after Chand.
- Asha goes on the first of the six days.
- Elan goes on Thursday.
- Fatima goes earlier in the week than Dolly.

Who goes on Friday?

solution.explanation: Asha Sunday, Chand Tuesday, Babu Wednesday, Elan Thursday. Monday and Friday remain; Fatima is earlier than Dolly, so Fatima Monday and Dolly Friday.
steps: Asha Sun, Chand Tue, Babu Wed, Elan Thu
Fatima before Dolly ⇒ Fatima Mon, Dolly Fri
solution.why_others_wrong: Fatima goes on Monday, Elan on Thursday and Babu on Wednesday.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four boxes P, Q, R and S have different weights. On a balance:
- P and Q together exactly balance R and S together.
- P and R together are heavier than Q and S together.
- P and S together are lighter than Q and R together.

Which box is the heaviest?

solution.concept: Add and subtract the balance relations
solution.explanation: Write P + Q = R + S (1), P + R > Q + S (2), P + S < Q + R (3). (2) − (1): R − Q > Q − R, so R > Q. (1) + (3): 2P + Q + S < 2R + Q + S, so R > P. From (1), R − P = Q − S, and R > P, so Q > S; also R > P and (2) + (1) give P > S. So R is heavier than P, Q and S.
steps: R > P > S (and Q > S) ⇒ R heaviest
solution.why_others_wrong: P and Q are each lighter than R; S is the lightest box.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who is the Coordinator?

solution.explanation: Kamini > Pratik > Naina > Lokesh occupy ranks 3–6, so Kamini is the Coordinator.
steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which subject does Lokesh teach?

steps: Madhav Principal–History, Oorja VP–Maths, Kamini Coordinator–Art, Pratik Senior Teacher–Science, Naina Teacher–Music, Lokesh Asst Teacher–English

questions.question_text: Who teaches Maths?

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following person – post – subject combinations is correct?

solution.explanation: Naina is the Teacher and teaches Music.

solution.why_others_wrong: Pratik is the Senior Teacher, Madhav the Principal and Kamini the Coordinator.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'X % Y & Z', how is Z related to X?

solution.concept: The wife of one's father is one's mother
solution.explanation: X is Y's daughter and Y is Z's husband, so Z is X's mother.
steps: X % Y: X is Y's daughter
Y & Z: Z is Y's wife ⇒ X's mother
solution.why_others_wrong: Z is a generation above X, so not her sister or daughter; nothing puts her two generations above.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'M ! N & O', how is O related to M?

solution.concept: A son's wife is a daughter-in-law
solution.explanation: M is N's father and N is O's husband, so O is the wife of M's son: M's daughter-in-law.
steps: M ! N: N is M's son (a husband is male)
N & O: O is N's wife ⇒ daughter-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: O is married into the family, not M's own daughter; M's wife is N's mother; O is a generation below M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'R ! S % T', how is T related to R?

solution.explanation: R is S's father; S is T's daughter, so T is S's other parent, her mother. T is therefore R's wife.
steps: R ! S: R is S's father
S % T: T is S's parent ⇒ mother
Father and mother of S ⇒ T is R's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: S is the daughter; T and R are S's two parents, so T is neither R's sister nor his mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Usha is the mother of Vinay. Vinay is the brother of Wamiqa, and Xavier is Wamiqa's husband. How is Usha related to Xavier?

solution.explanation: Vinay and Wamiqa are siblings, so Usha is Wamiqa's mother too. Xavier is Wamiqa's husband, so Usha is his mother-in-law.
steps: Usha = mother of Vinay and Wamiqa
solution.why_others_wrong: Xavier is not Usha's own son; she is a generation above him, so not his sister-in-law; an aunt is a parent's sister.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Deepak is the only son of Eshwar. Geeta is Deepak's sister, and Farida is Geeta's daughter. How is Deepak related to Farida?

solution.explanation: Deepak is the brother of Farida's mother Geeta, so he is Farida's (maternal) uncle.
solution.why_others_wrong: Farida's father is Geeta's husband; Deepak is a generation above Farida, so not her brother; her grandfather is Eshwar.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Hari is the husband of Ila. Ila's only son is Jai, and Jai's wife is Kiya. Lina is Kiya's daughter. How is Hari related to Lina?

solution.explanation: Jai is the son of Hari and Ila, and Lina is the daughter of Jai and his wife Kiya. Hari is Lina's father's father: her grandfather.
steps: Lina = Jai's daughter ⇒ Hari is her grandfather
solution.why_others_wrong: Lina's father is Jai; Hari is two generations above her; he is Kiya's father-in-law, not Lina's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Looking at the photograph of a woman, Kunal said, "Her husband's mother is the only sister of my father." How is the woman related to Kunal?

solution.concept: Collapse the phrase from the inside out
solution.explanation: The only sister of Kunal's father is Kunal's paternal aunt. Her son, the woman's husband, is Kunal's cousin, so the woman is the wife of Kunal's cousin.
solution.why_others_wrong: She is not a child of Kunal's parents; the aunt is her mother-in-law, not her; she is related to Kunal only by marriage, so not his own cousin.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Wife of his cousin

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

options.text: A is the uncle of C
D is the husband of B
A is the son of D

solution.explanation: A is B's brother; B is C's mother; C is D's daughter, so D is C's father and B's husband. So A is C's maternal uncle, D is B's husband and C is a girl — all true. A is B's brother, i.e. D's brother-in-law, not D's son.
steps: A @ B, B # C ⇒ A is C's maternal uncle
C $ D with B the mother ⇒ D is the father, B's husband
A is D's brother-in-law ⇒ 'son of D' is false
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three statements follow directly from the code.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is the son of D

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Om is the father of Usha, and Tia is Usha's daughter. Usha's only sibling is Varun, and Wanda is Varun's wife. How is Wanda related to Tia?

solution.explanation: Varun is the brother of Tia's mother Usha, i.e. Tia's maternal uncle. Wanda, his wife, is Tia's aunt.
solution.why_others_wrong: Tia's mother is Usha; Wanda is Usha's sister-in-law, not Tia's; Tia's grandmother is Om's wife.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Qasim related to Pranav?

solution.explanation: Pranav's father Mehul is Naina's brother, and Qasim is Naina's husband, so Qasim is Pranav's uncle (paternal aunt's husband).
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
Qasim = husband of Pranav's father's sister ⇒ uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Pranav's father is Mehul; Qasim's child Riya is Pranav's cousin; his grandfather is Kartik.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Leela related to Riya?

solution.explanation: Riya's mother is Naina (Qasim's wife), and Naina is Leela's daughter, so Leela is Riya's grandmother.
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
solution.why_others_wrong: Riya's mother is Naina; Leela is two generations above Riya; she is Qasim's mother-in-law, not Riya's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Ojasvi related to Naina?

solution.explanation: Ojasvi is married to Mehul, Naina's brother, so Ojasvi is Naina's sister-in-law.
steps: Kartik + Leela → Mehul (+ Ojasvi) → Pranav; Naina (+ Qasim) → Riya
solution.why_others_wrong: Ojasvi has different parents from Naina; she is in Naina's generation, so not her mother-in-law; cousins share grandparents.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sahil is the only son-in-law of Rohan's paternal grandfather. Rohan's father has exactly one sibling, and every person mentioned has only one spouse. How is Sahil related to Rohan?

solution.concept: A son-in-law must be married to a daughter
solution.explanation: A son-in-law of Rohan's grandfather is married to one of the grandfather's daughters. The grandfather's children are Rohan's father and his only sibling, so that sibling is a daughter: Rohan's paternal aunt. Sahil is her husband, i.e. Rohan's uncle.
steps: Only sibling of Rohan's father ⇒ that daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Rohan's father is a son of the grandfather, not a son-in-law; Sahil is a generation above Rohan, so not his brother-in-law or cousin.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Uncle (husband of his father's sister)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Test every option; the gender of P must be fixed
solution.explanation: In 'P ™ Q ® S', P is Q's daughter and Q is S's brother, so P is the daughter of S's brother: S's niece. In 'S ® Q © P', S is the brother of P's mother, but P's gender is unknown (nephew or niece). 'P ® Q ™ S' makes P S's son, and 'S © Q ® P' makes S P's mother.
steps: Option 1: daughter of S's brother ⇒ niece ✓
solution.why_others_wrong: The second does not fix P's gender; the third and fourth give son and mother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Early one morning, Kavya walked straight towards the sun. She then turned to her left and kept walking. In which direction was she walking then?

solution.concept: The morning sun is in the east
solution.explanation: Walking towards the morning sun means walking east. A left turn from east points north.
solution.why_others_wrong: South is a right turn from east; West is away from the sun; East ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between the depot and stop B, and in which direction is B from the depot?

solution.explanation: B is 6 km east and 8 km north of D: √(36 + 64) = 10 km, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '10 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '14 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the end point F from the depot in a straight line, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement of the whole trip
solution.explanation: East: 6 − 12 + 10 = 4 km; north: 8 − 5 = 3 km. √(16 + 9) = 5 km, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: '5 km, North-West' mixes up east and west; '5 km, South-West' gives the direction of the start from the end point; '7 km, North-East' adds the two components instead of using Pythagoras.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is stop C with respect to stop F?

solution.explanation: C (−6, 8) − F (4, 3) = (−10, 5): west and north, so C is north-west of F.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is F's direction from C; North-East misreads C as east of F; West ignores the 5 km north component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which stop is nearest to the depot in a straight line?

solution.explanation: Distances from D: A 6 km, B 10 km, C 10 km, E √45 ≈ 6.7 km, F 5 km. F is nearest.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is 6 km, E about 6.7 km and B 10 km away.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A girl is facing south-east. She turns 135° anticlockwise three times in a row. Which direction is she facing now?

solution.explanation: Three turns of 135° make 405° anticlockwise, which is a full circle plus 45°. 45° anticlockwise from south-east is east.
solution.why_others_wrong: North and South-West come from stopping after one or two turns; South turns the last 45° the other way.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At about 5 pm, Anil and Bhanu were walking straight towards each other on a road. Anil's shadow fell directly behind him. In which direction was Bhanu walking?

solution.explanation: At 5 pm the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Anil's shadow was behind him, so Anil was walking west, towards the sun. Bhanu, walking towards Anil, was walking east.
steps: Shadow behind Anil ⇒ Anil walks west
Bhanu walks the opposite way ⇒ east
solution.why_others_wrong: West is Anil's direction; North and South are at right angles to the road's direction.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sneha cycles 7 km towards the north, turns right and cycles 5 km, turns left and cycles 4 km, turns right and cycles 9 km, and then turns right again and cycles 11 km. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: North and south legs may cancel
solution.explanation: North 7 + 4 = 11, then south 11: the north–south parts cancel. East 5 + 9 = 14 km. She is 14 km due east of the start.
steps: Turn right from north ⇒ east: 5 km → (5, 7)
Turn left from east ⇒ north: 4 km → (5, 11)
Turn right from north ⇒ east: 9 km → (14, 11)
Turn right from east ⇒ south: 11 km → (14, 0)
solution.why_others_wrong: West mixes up the right turns; 36 km adds every leg; 11 km, South is only the last leg.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which point lies exactly midway between K and J?

solution.concept: Drop M onto the line KJ
solution.explanation: M = (5, 5) is the midpoint of KL. N is 5 m south of M, i.e. (5, 0), which is exactly halfway along KJ from (0, 0) to (10, 0).
solution.why_others_wrong: M is 5 m north of KJ, O is 2 m west of K's north–south line, and L is 10 m north of J.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between K and M, and in which direction is M from K?

solution.explanation: M is the midpoint of KL, and L is 10 m east and 10 m north of K, so M is 5 m east and 5 m north of K: 5√2 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5 m, North ignores the east part; 10 m takes the full side length; South-West is K's direction from M.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is L from O, and in which direction is L from O?

solution.explanation: O = (−2, 5) and L = (10, 10): L is 12 m east and 5 m north of O, √(144 + 25) = 13 m, north-east.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West is O's direction from L; 17 m adds the two parts; 12 m, East ignores the north part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, SALT is written as WEPX. How is CORN written in that code language?

solution.concept: Every letter moves forward by the same number of places
solution.explanation: S→W, A→E, L→P, T→X: every letter moves 4 places forward. C→G, O→S, R→V, N→R: GSVR.
solution.why_others_wrong: YKNJ moves the letters back; GSVQ moves N only 3 places; HTWS moves every letter 5 places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 5274 is written as 6385 and 3916 is written as 4027. How is 8093 written in that code?

steps: Each digit +1, keeping only the units digit
solution.why_others_wrong: 7982 subtracts 1; 9105 adds 2 to the last digit; 3909 reverses the number and changes nothing else.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LEMON is written as LMKCJ and GRAPE is written as CNYPE. How is MELON written in that code?

solution.concept: Reverse, then move each letter back
solution.explanation: LEMON reversed is NOMEL; each letter moved 2 places back: L M K C J. GRAPE → EPARG → C N Y P E. MELON → NOLEM → L M J C K.
solution.why_others_wrong: KCJML shifts without reversing; PQNGO moves the letters forward; LMJCL moves the last letter back only once.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 4815 is written as 3366 and 2967 is written as 8547. How is 7302 written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap the halves, then +2 and −2 alternately
solution.explanation: 4815: the two halves are interchanged → 1548; then the 1st and 3rd digits get +2 and the 2nd and 4th get −2: 3 3 6 6. 2967 → 6729 → 8 5 4 7. 7302 → 0273 → 0+2 = 2, 2−2 = 0, 7+2 = 9, 3−2 = 1: 2091.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9180 applies the +2/−2 without swapping; 0273 only swaps; 2093 adds 2 to the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is 'BRIDGE' written in this code?

solution.explanation: BRIDGE: last letter E, 6 letters, B + 2 = D, giving E6D. Six is even, so the code is reversed: D6E.
solution.why_others_wrong: E6D forgets the reversal; D6F reverses but shifts the wrong letter; E6B does not shift B.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is 'STAMP' written in this code?

solution.explanation: STAMP: last letter P, 5 letters, S + 2 = U. Five is odd, so the code stays P5U.
solution.why_others_wrong: U5P reverses an odd-length code; P5T moves S only one place; R5U shifts the last letter.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words is written as 'K7R' in this code?

solution.explanation: K7R is not reversed only if the word has an odd number of letters: 7 letters, ending in K, with first letter R − 2 = P. PADLOCK fits. SHAMROCK → U8K, PARK → R4K, PLUCK → K5R.
steps: Last letter K, first letter P, 7 letters ⇒ PADLOCK
solution.why_others_wrong: SHAMROCK has 8 letters and starts with S; PARK has 4 letters (code reversed); PLUCK has 5.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 3rd to the left of the 6th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Convert a right-end position, then move left
solution.explanation: The 6th from the right is the 12th from the left (F). Three places to its left is the 9th element: K.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many numbers in the arrangement are immediately followed by a letter?

solution.concept: Look at the right neighbour of every number
solution.explanation: Numbers and their right neighbours: 3 %, 8 A, 5 K, 1 F, 7 I, 2 Y. Followed by a letter: 8 A, 5 K, 1 F, 7 I, 2 Y — 5.
steps: Keep those with a letter on the right

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the numbers are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 7th from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without numbers: W % H A @ K £ F I # Y. The 7th from the left is £.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Which term should replace the question mark in the series?

C3, F6, I9, L12, ?

solution.concept: The number is the letter's position
solution.explanation: The letters move 3 places forward each time (C, F, I, L, O) and each number is its letter's position (3, 6, 9, 12, 15). The next term is O15.
solution.why_others_wrong: O14 and N15 break the link between the letter and its position; P15 moves the letter 4 places.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

T % A 6 # E @ 9 U $ R I ¥ 4 O & B

How many vowels in the arrangement are immediately followed by a symbol?

solution.concept: Look at the right neighbour of every vowel

questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Bina is the only sister of Ankit's father.

Conclusions:
I. Bina is Ankit's aunt.
II. Ankit's father has no brother.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The sister of one's father is one's aunt, so I follows. Being the only sister means Ankit's father has no other sister; it says nothing about brothers, so II does not follow.
steps: 'Only sister' says nothing about brothers ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both read 'only sister' as 'only sibling'; Neither misses the direct relation.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The company's revenue this year was the highest in its history.

Conclusions:
I. The company made a profit this year.
II. The company's revenue will be higher next year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Revenue is what the company earned from sales; profit also depends on its costs, which are not given, so I does not follow. A record this year says nothing certain about next year, so II does not follow.
steps: Revenue ≠ profit ⇒ I does not follow
No information about next year ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Each other option treats record revenue as if it guaranteed profit or future growth.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A club has 60 members. 25 of them play tennis, and every member who plays tennis also swims. 20 members neither play tennis nor swim.

Conclusions:
I. More members of the club play tennis than swim.
II. Exactly 15 members of the club swim but do not play tennis.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The 40 members who do something all swim (tennis players swim too, and the rest of the 40 must swim). So 40 swim, of whom 25 also play tennis: 40 − 25 = 15 swim without playing tennis (II). Since 40 swim and 25 play tennis, I is false.
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both reverse the comparison; Neither ignores the direct count.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The bus fare from a village to the town is ₹30 per passenger. An auto-rickshaw makes the same trip for ₹90, whether it carries one, two or three passengers.

Conclusions:
I. For three people travelling together, the auto-rickshaw costs the same as the bus.
II. For two people travelling together, the bus is cheaper than the auto-rickshaw.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Three people pay 3 × ₹30 = ₹90 by bus, the same as the auto-rickshaw (I). Two people pay ₹60 by bus, less than ₹90 (II).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two direct comparisons.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Some of the bank's branches open on Sundays. Every branch of the bank that opens on Sundays has a cash-deposit machine.

Conclusions:
I. Some of the bank's branches that have a cash-deposit machine open on Sundays.
II. Every branch of the bank that has a cash-deposit machine opens on Sundays.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The branches that open on Sundays exist and all have cash-deposit machines, so some branches with machines open on Sundays (I). 'Every Sunday branch has a machine' cannot be reversed: branches with machines may also be closed on Sundays, so II does not follow.
steps: Some branches open on Sundays; all of them have machines ⇒ I
Converse of an 'every' statement ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both reverse the 'every' statement; Neither misses the 'some' conclusion.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Claim: Keeping the school library open during the lunch break will increase the number of books that students borrow.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

options.text: The library has more than 5,000 books
At present the library is open only during class hours, when most students cannot visit it
Some students bring their own books to school

solution.concept: Strengthen: show that access is the obstacle now
solution.explanation: If students borrow few books because the library is open only when they are in class, opening it at lunch removes that obstacle, so more books are likely to be borrowed.
steps: Claim: more opening time ⇒ more borrowing
Strengthener: students cannot visit at present
solution.why_others_wrong: The size of the collection and the length of the break do not show that students will come; students with their own books are, if anything, less likely to borrow.
solution.final_answer: Option C: At present the library is open only during class hours, when most students cannot visit it

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A recipe that serves 4 people needs 300 g of rice. Neha is making the same recipe for 10 people, using rice in the same proportion.

Which of the following can be inferred?

solution.concept: Scale in proportion to the number of people
solution.explanation: Rice per person = 300 ÷ 4 = 75 g, so 10 people need 75 × 10 = 750 g.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 g doubles the recipe; 1,200 g quadruples it; 3 kg multiplies by ten instead of by 10 ÷ 4.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Neha needs 750 g of rice

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Several elderly residents of a housing society have slipped and fallen on the society's staircase, whose steps are worn smooth and have no handrail.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ask the elderly residents to stay indoors
Stop visitors from using the staircase
Fit handrails and anti-slip strips on the staircase

solution.concept: Remove the cause of the falls
solution.explanation: The falls are caused by smooth steps with nothing to hold. Handrails and anti-slip strips fix both causes.
solution.why_others_wrong: Keeping residents indoors or closing the staircase is impractical; stopping visitors does not make the steps safer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Fit handrails and anti-slip strips on the staircase

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Claim: A café's new menu is popular with its customers, because the café's sales rose by 40% in the first week after the new menu was introduced.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the claim?

options.text: The new menu has more vegetarian dishes than the old one
The café is located near a college
During that first week, the café gave a 50% discount on every item to celebrate the new menu
The café's owner designed the new menu herself

solution.concept: Weaken: give another reason for the rise
solution.explanation: A half-price offer in the same week could explain the jump in sales by itself, so the rise does not show that customers like the new menu.
steps: Weakener: 50% discount in the same week
solution.why_others_wrong: The kind of dishes, the location and who designed the menu do not explain a sudden one-week rise.
solution.final_answer: Option C: During that first week, the café gave a 50% discount on every item to celebrate the new menu

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Many small traders in a town are losing sales because they accept only cash, while more and more customers want to pay digitally.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Ban digital payments in the town
Ask customers to carry more cash
Help the traders open free QR-code payment accounts with their banks and show them how to use them
Close the shops that accept only cash

solution.concept: Enable the traders rather than restrict the customers
solution.explanation: Traders lose sales because they cannot accept digital payments. Helping them start accepting such payments removes the problem.
solution.why_others_wrong: Banning digital payments or telling customers to carry cash goes against what customers want; closing shops punishes the traders.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Help the traders open free QR-code payment accounts with their banks and show them how to use them

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A museum gives free entry to children under 12 years of age and to people over 60. All other visitors pay ₹50 each. On Sunday, a family visited the museum: a grandmother aged 65, two parents aged 38 and 36, and two children aged 12 and 8.

Which of the following can be inferred?

options.text: The family paid ₹100 in all for entry
The family paid ₹200 in all for entry
The family paid ₹250 in all for entry
The family paid ₹150 in all for entry

solution.explanation: The grandmother (over 60) and the 8-year-old (under 12) enter free. The two parents and the 12-year-old (who is not under 12) pay ₹50 each: ₹150.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹100 treats the 12-year-old as under 12; ₹200 charges the grandmother or the younger child; ₹250 charges everyone.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The family paid ₹150 in all for entry

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Countries with more mobile phones per person have higher average incomes. So giving free mobile phones to families in the state's poorest districts will raise their incomes.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: A trial last year that gave free phones to 10,000 families in two of the poorest districts found no change in their incomes after a year, compared with similar families who did not get phones
Mobile phones have become cheaper in recent years
Most people in the poorest districts work in farming
Several companies sell mobile phones in the state

solution.concept: Weaken: direct evidence against the predicted effect
solution.explanation: The argument predicts that free phones will raise incomes. A controlled trial in the same kind of districts found no effect, which directly undercuts the prediction drawn from a country-level link.
solution.why_others_wrong: Cheaper phones, the main occupation and the number of sellers do not show whether phones raise incomes.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A trial last year that gave free phones to 10,000 families in two of the poorest districts found no change in their incomes after a year, compared with similar families who did not get phones

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The hospital's new rule that doctors must wash their hands before examining each patient is the reason infections among its patients fell by 30% this year.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: The hospital made no other change this year in its cleaning, staffing or kinds of patients, and similar hospitals without the rule saw no fall in infections
Hand-washing takes doctors less than a minute
Doctors at the hospital agreed with the new rule

solution.explanation: If nothing else changed at the hospital and comparable hospitals without the rule saw no fall, the new rule is the most likely reason for the drop in infections.
steps: Strengthener: no other change; no fall elsewhere
solution.why_others_wrong: The time hand-washing takes, the hospital's size and doctors' agreement do not link the rule to the fall.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The hospital made no other change this year in its cleaning, staffing or kinds of patients, and similar hospitals without the rule saw no fall in infections

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: Five lectures — on Economics, History, Law, Maths and Physics — are held one after another on a day. Law is held immediately after History. Maths is the third lecture. Physics is held at some time before Economics.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Physics is held immediately before Economics

solution.concept: Find every arrangement, then pick what holds in all
solution.explanation: History–Law must take places 1–2 or 4–5 (Maths is 3rd). If they are 1–2, Physics and Economics are 4th and 5th; if they are 4–5, Physics and Economics are 1st and 2nd. In both cases Physics comes immediately before Economics.
steps: Case 1: History, Law, Maths, Physics, Economics
Case 2: Physics, Economics, Maths, History, Law
Common to both: Physics just before Economics
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options holds in only one of the two possible orders.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Physics is held immediately before Economics

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: A survey found that the city's buses run almost empty between 11 am and 4 pm but are badly overcrowded during the morning and evening peak hours.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Stop all bus services between 11 am and 4 pm
Buy enough new buses to double the fleet at once
Raise fares sharply during peak hours to keep people off the buses
Shift some buses from the afternoon schedule to the peak hours, and offer lower fares in the afternoon

solution.concept: Match supply to demand at low cost
solution.explanation: Buses are idle in the afternoon and short at peak hours. Moving buses to the peak hours uses the existing fleet better, and cheaper afternoon fares can draw some travellers away from the peaks.
steps: Problem: mismatch between bus supply and demand
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping afternoon buses strands those who travel then; doubling the fleet is costly and leaves more empty buses; sharp peak fares penalise people who must travel at those hours.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Shift some buses from the afternoon schedule to the peak hours, and offer lower fares in the afternoon

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Patients who choose Dr Mehta for knee surgery recover faster than the patients of the other knee surgeons at the hospital. So Dr Mehta is the hospital's best knee surgeon.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: Dr Mehta has worked at the hospital for ten years
The hospital has four knee surgeons
Dr Mehta's patients pay the same fees as other patients
Dr Mehta operates mostly on young athletes with minor injuries, while the other surgeons treat most of the elderly patients with severe knee damage

solution.concept: Weaken: the groups being compared differ
solution.explanation: Young patients with minor injuries recover faster whoever operates on them. If Dr Mehta's patients are mostly such cases, their faster recovery does not show that he is the best surgeon.
steps: Evidence: faster recovery of Dr Mehta's patients
Weakener: his patients are easier cases
solution.why_others_wrong: Years of service, the number of surgeons and fees do not explain the difference in recovery.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Dr Mehta operates mostly on young athletes with minor injuries, while the other surgeons treat most of the elderly patients with severe knee damage

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: In a class, the average mark of the 20 boys is 60, and the average mark of the 30 girls is 70. There are no other students in the class.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: The average mark of the whole class is 66
The average mark of the whole class is 65
At least one girl scored more than 70
Every girl scored more than every boy

solution.concept: A combined average is weighted by group size
solution.explanation: Total marks = 20 × 60 + 30 × 70 = 1,200 + 2,100 = 3,300 for 50 students: average 66.
solution.why_others_wrong: 65 averages the two averages without weighting; every girl could have scored exactly 70; averages say nothing about every individual.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The average mark of the whole class is 66

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: An audit found that the city's government hospitals often run out of essential medicines because each hospital places its own orders late and in small quantities.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Stop giving free medicines at the hospitals
Ask patients to bring their own medicines
Set up a central system that tracks every hospital's stock and places orders automatically before stocks run low
Order a five-year stock of every medicine at once

solution.concept: Fix the ordering process that causes the shortage
solution.explanation: Shortages come from late, small orders by each hospital. Central tracking with automatic reordering keeps stocks up without the waste of huge one-time purchases.
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping free medicines or shifting the burden to patients defeats the purpose of the hospitals; a five-year stock would expire and waste money.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Set up a central system that tracks every hospital's stock and places orders automatically before stocks run low
